narrative:
The model predicted a 66% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the third decile, noticeably lower than the average of accepted students (around the sixth and fifth deciles respectively). These weaker relative performances in law school coursework signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the next most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 43, your score sits comfortably above the average of 37 among accepted students, which helped pull the prediction back toward success. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the impact of your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.0 was slightly below the accepted average of 3.23, your middle family income is fairly typical, and your plan to attend full-time matches what nearly all accepted students do. Gender and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the bar exam preparation courses or seeking additional support. Raising your class standing in future years or gaining targeted bar exam experience could meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
